reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: A selective failure of erythropoiesis producing severe anaemia with reticulocytopenia while white cells and platelets are preserved
The bone marrow shows a marked reduction or absence of erythroid precursors with otherwise normal cellularity
Parvovirus B19 is a classic cause, especially in immunocompromised patients or those with a shortened red cell lifespan such as haemolytic anaemias
A strong association exists with thymoma, and cross-sectional chest imaging should be performed to look for a mediastinal mass
Other secondary causes include lymphoproliferative disorders (notably large granular lymphocytic leukaemia), autoimmune disease, drugs and pregnancy
Anti-erythropoietin antibodies are a recognised cause in patients previously treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents
Management addresses the underlying cause, for example thymectomy, antiviral immunoglobulin for parvovirus, or immunosuppression for immune-mediated disease
reference.pathophysiology: Pure red cell aplasia results from a selective arrest of erythroid precursor development in the bone marrow, sparing the granulocytic and megakaryocytic lineages. Several mechanisms converge on this outcome: direct viral cytotoxicity to erythroid progenitors by parvovirus B19, which infects them via the P antigen; T-cell or antibody-mediated immune attack on erythroid precursors as in thymoma-associated and large granular lymphocytic leukaemia-associated disease; and neutralising antibodies against erythropoietin or its receptor. The congenital form, Diamond-Blackfan anaemia, arises from ribosomal protein gene defects impairing erythroid maturation. The common endpoint is failed red cell production with preserved reticulocyte-poor anaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Aplastic anaemia (pancytopenia rather than isolated anaemia)
Acute parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis in haemolytic anaemia
Anaemia of chronic disease or renal failure
Congenital Diamond-Blackfan anaemia in the young
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing absent erythroid precursors
Parvovirus B19 PCR, particularly in immunocompromised patients
Cross-sectional chest imaging to detect thymoma
Peripheral blood immunophenotyping and T-cell clonality for large granular lymphocytic leukaemia
Autoimmune screen and review of drug and erythropoietin exposure
redFlags: Profound symptomatic anaemia requiring urgent transfusion
A mediastinal mass on imaging suggesting thymoma
Features of an underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder
Persistent aplasia despite treatment suggesting a missed cause
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause; parvovirus-related and drug-related cases often recover once the trigger is removed or treated, thymoma-associated disease may improve after thymectomy, and idiopathic or immune forms frequently need ongoing immunosuppression.
pitfalls: Overlooking thymoma by not imaging the chest
Missing parvovirus B19 in an immunocompromised or haemolytic patient
Failing to identify an underlying large granular lymphocytic leukaemia
Not reviewing recent drugs or erythropoietin exposure as a reversible cause
